idiom_name: dirty bit plus a recompute-on-read accessor (language-neutral)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral blueprint: keep the primary data, the derived value and one flag per cache together behind an accessor; every mutating operation sets the flag, and the accessor recomputes only when it is set, publishes the result and then clears the flag. The flag starts set, because a fresh object has no valid cache. The invariant to enforce is completeness - no path may change primary data without marking - so the mutators should funnel through a single narrow API per type. When a change to one element invalidates derived values of dependents (a parent's movement affecting its children), propagate the dirty state through the traversal that already visits them rather than walking and marking the dependents eagerly. Under concurrency, publish the cache first, then clear the flag with release semantics (or equivalent); a reader uses acquire semantics before reading the cache. Use a compare-and-swap TryConsumeDirty to ensure exactly one thread does the recomputation: if dirty, atomically flip to clean before recomputing; if another thread beat you, return the in-progress result or block. For CDC pipelines, the 'processed offset' map is a second-level dirty flag: it records which WAL positions have been applied, enabling idempotent restart after any outage.
code_sketch:
state := { primary, derived, dirty = true }

mutate(state, change):
    apply(primary, change)
    state.dirty = true                    # mark, never recompute here

read_derived(state):
    if state.dirty:
        state.derived = compute(primary)  # publish
        state.dirty = false               # then clear
    return state.derived

# concurrent form (try-consume):
read_derived_concurrent(state):
    if !state.dirty:
        return state.derived
    if state.try_consume_dirty():         # CAS: dirty->clean, returns true only for winner
        state.derived = compute(primary)
        state.dirty = false               # publish under lock or atomic op
    return state.derived

# dependents: pass parent_dirty down the traversal; do not walk and mark them
pitfalls: A single mutation path that forgets to mark makes the cache stale forever with no visible error - the marking must live in one choke point per type.
Clearing the flag before the recomputation succeeded (or before the result is published) turns a temporary failure into permanent staleness.
Recursively marking every dependent on each mutation replaces an O(1) mark with an O(n) walk; thread the dirty state through the traversal instead.
No bound on how long the deferral may last: without a checkpoint, background flush or auto-save, deferred persistence work can be lost entirely.

A plain volatile boolean is insufficient for cross-thread coordination: it does not guarantee memory visibility or ordering, and a reader may observe a clean flag before the writer's cache write is visible - use atomic operations or a critical section around both the flag and the cache together.

Using AtomicBoolean alone does not guarantee coherence between the flag and the data it guards: if setDirty() does dirty.set(true) and arr[index] = value in separate statements, a reader can see dirty=false with arr[index] still stale. Both operations must be inside the same synchronized block or use compare-and-swap on a compound state object.
Double-checked locking without volatile/atomic semantics on the flag produces a torn read: the fast path reads a clean flag but the cache may still be in flight from a concurrent recomputation.

Hibernate bytecode enhancement pitfall: the entity snapshot is still held in the PersistenceContext even with self-tracking enabled, so the memory saving is smaller than expected; also, the deprecated hibernate-enhance-maven-plugin must not be confused with the JPA @Entity annotation enhancement which does NOT include dirty tracking.

EF Core pitfall: HasChanges() triggers DetectChanges() internally; calling both in sequence is redundant; read-only transactions (@Transactional(readOnly=true)) suppress snapshot creation and dirty detection entirely - modifications made in that scope are silently ignored unless SaveChanges is called with explicit EntityState manipulation.

Extended PersistenceContext memory: a Hibernate PC is an in-memory first-level cache that grows until the EntityManager is closed or explicitly cleared; for long-running conversations (e.g. wizard UIs) this can cause OutOfMemoryException - use entity-manager-per-request or periodic EntityManager.clear() with reattachment.

Snapshot corruption: when the dirty flag defers persistence work (save-on-close, background flush), a crash mid-deferral loses all dirty changes; auto-save, transactional outbox, or write-ahead logging compensates - but these add complexity comparable to event sourcing, at which point event sourcing may be the better choice.

Hysteresis-free toggling: a flag that is set and cleared on every change for a value that changes every frame buys nothing and adds overhead; use hysteresis (e.g. physics sleeping with a velocity threshold) or simply do not cache when the change frequency approaches the read frequency.

CDC schema drift: nullable field absence or renamed columns cause downstream consumers to reject events; Debezium's ExpandContract migration strategy avoids breaking changes but requires careful coordination across teams.

CDC binlog retention: MySQL binlog retention means a slow or dead consumer loses offsets and requires a full resync; configure gtid_mode and semi-synchronous replication to bound the window of data loss.

Noita-style dirty rectangle shrinking: maintaining a single dirty bounding rect that grows as particles move but never shrinks correctly causes the scan region to balloon to the whole world; use two rects (previous-frame and per-frame delta) and union them to get the true dirty region, then replace previous with current for the next frame.

CDC exactly-once delivery gap: Debezium's streaming phase achieves at-least-once with transactional offset commits; the snapshot phase can produce duplicates on failure/restart; downstream consumers must be idempotent or use upsert semantics keyed on the event's source position to survive duplicates.

Dirty rect bookkeeping overhead: for very sparse worlds (few particles moving in a large grid), the per-cell dirty flag array itself consumes significant memory; use a sparse set or hash-based approach instead of a full-world grid of dirty booleans.

Vulkan scene graph topological ordering failure: if nodes are not stored in parent-before-child order, a single-pass dirty-flag propagation produces incorrect world matrices on frames after a node is added; the glTF loader must topologically sort nodes at load time.

MobX computed non-observation: when a computed value is not observed by any reaction it is eligible for garbage collection and its cache is dropped; accessing it again triggers full recomputation; wrapping a computed in a manual reaction that sets a dirty flag is redundant and introduces the correctness risk the framework already handles.

Wrong move: assuming the framework clears the flag for you (Unity's Transform.hasChanged stays set once raised) -> every later poll reports 'dirty', the flag stays stuck and the deferral degenerates into recomputing every frame -> instead clear it yourself right after handling the change (transform.hasChanged = false), which defines the detection window.

Wrong move: invalidating from only the write path you remembered, or letting a TTL/expiry mask the misses -> the other write paths serve stale derived data silently and shortening the expiry only hides the bug longer -> instead funnel every mutation through one choke point, fire invalidation after the source transaction commits, and alert on observed staleness.

Wrong move: calling the forced flush (WPF UpdateLayout, a synchronous reflow) after every small property change -> each change pays the full recomputation cost, worse than eager recomputation because the flag bookkeeping is still there -> instead let invalidations batch to the next natural pass and force a synchronous pass only when geometry is genuinely needed now.
